title: When a Bedside Result Needs Backup: Urine hCG, Fingerstick Creatinine and Cardiac Markers
summary: Learn why a urine pregnancy strip is read by its own device instructions and when a negative needs confirming, why borderline fingerstick creatinine goes to the central lab, what point-of-care cardiac markers did and did not change in a large trial, and what CLIA requires before a new test reports results.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 7 Hits 6 (urine hCG follows the named assay), 9 (POCT cardiac markers) and 10 (method validation) and Traps 3 (cardiac markers in the ED) and 5 (borderline fingerstick creatinine). Checked against Gnoth and Johnson 2014 (read via a page-fetch tool), Priyadarshini 2022, Winder 2017, Nataatmadja 2020, Lemoine 2022, the RATPAC trial (Goodacre 2011; abstracts only, via Europe PMC; the NIHR full report returned HTTP 403), Rooney and Schilling 2014, Shaw 2016, Khan 2019, and 42 CFR 493.15 and 493.1253 (eCFR version 2026-10-01). Not taught as fact: the QuickVue 25 mIU/mL figure (the QuidelOrtho product page could not be retrieved: redirect then 404), the “10–20 specimens” validation size for dipsticks (no source read states it; CLIA lists non-automated dipsticks as waived, see register flag rv-ch7-dipstick-validation-size), the “not ideal” fingerstick quote, and the Number Vault rows (Table 1 not claimed). Hit 9 is qualified: RATPAC found faster discharge and shorter median but not mean stay, no difference in adverse events, and higher cost (register flag rv-ch7-poc-cardiac-efficiency). US-only regulatory content; Philippine rules are not covered.

objectives: Explain why a qualitative urine hCG result is interpreted by the named device’s instructions, and list causes of a false-negative strip.
Decide when a point-of-care creatinine result should be confirmed in the central laboratory.
Describe what point-of-care cardiac markers changed and did not change in a randomised trial, and what CLIA requires before a new non-waived test reports results.

scenes.title: Fast answers, fair questions
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: an emergency department has three bedside results. (1) A urine pregnancy strip is negative, but the patient’s uterus is much larger than expected and molar pregnancy is suspected. (2) A fingerstick creatinine before contrast CT sits right at the department’s decision cut-off. (3) The ED manager says the new point-of-care cardiac marker panel will “save lives in chest pain”. A fourth card: the lab is about to bring in a new point-of-care analyzer. Question token: “Trust it, confirm it, or verify it first?”

cues.text: Three bedside results in one emergency department. A urine pregnancy strip is negative, yet the uterus is far too large and a molar pregnancy is suspected.
A fingerstick creatinine before a contrast scan lands right on the cut-off. And the manager says the new bedside cardiac panel will save lives.
Meanwhile a new bedside analyzer is arriving. Trust it, confirm it, or verify it first?

props.label: Trust it, confirm it, or verify it first?

scenes.title: A urine hCG strip reads its own threshold
scenes.altText: Schematic lateral-flow strip: antibodies on the strip capture hCG in urine and form a visible line. Card 1: detection thresholds are device-specific — one review reports most kits detect hCG at about 25–50 mIU/mL, others from 15 to 100 mIU/mL; a laboratory study of German home tests found about half did not reach their claimed sensitivity. Card 2 (US CLIA): visual colour-comparison urine pregnancy tests are on the waived list (42 CFR 493.15(c)(4)), and a waived laboratory must follow the manufacturer’s instructions (493.15(e)). Token: “The threshold belongs to THAT device — read its insert.” Token: “Quantitative serum hCG = separate test, own lab intervals.”

cues.text: A qualitative urine pregnancy strip uses antibodies against hCG. If enough hCG is present, a line appears. There is no number on the result, only a line or no line.

How much hCG is enough depends on the device. Most kits detect around twenty-five to fifty units per litre, but some claim fifteen and others need a hundred. In one laboratory study, about half of the home tests checked did not reach their claimed sensitivity.

Under US CLIA, visual urine pregnancy tests are waived tests, and a waived laboratory must follow the manufacturer’s instructions. So the threshold and how to read the strip come from that device’s insert.
A quantitative serum hCG is a different test with its own laboratory intervals. Keep the two apart.

scenes.title: When the fast answer misleads
scenes.altText: Card “False-negative urine hCG”: (a) testing too early, before enough hCG is in urine, is the most common cause of a falsely negative home test; (b) hook effect: very high hCG (for example in molar pregnancy) can give a falsely negative strip; diluting the urine before repeating often overcomes it; (c) hCG variants such as the beta-core fragment can predominate and fail to form the antibody sandwich. Action token: clinical picture does not fit → repeat on diluted urine and confirm; if molar pregnancy is suspected, tell the lab so quantitative hCG is run on a diluted sample. Card “Fingerstick creatinine”: in one CKD clinic study a handheld device read about 12.7 µmol/L higher than plasma on average and misclassified patients across all CKD stages, with imprecision as well as bias; in another, eGFR below 60 was correctly classified in 84% with capillary blood versus 100% with the laboratory method. Action token: near a decision cut-off → confirm in the central laboratory.

cues.text: A negative strip is not always a negative pregnancy. The commonest cause is testing too early, before enough hCG reaches the urine.

Very high hCG, as in a molar pregnancy, can swamp the antibodies and give a false negative: the hook effect. Diluting the urine often fixes it. Unusual hCG fragments can also escape the antibody sandwich.
So when the picture does not fit, repeat on diluted urine and confirm. If a mole is suspected, tell the lab so the quantitative test is run on a diluted sample.

Fingerstick creatinine has its own limits. In one kidney clinic study a handheld meter read higher than plasma and misclassified patients at every kidney disease stage. In another, it placed patients below an eGFR of sixty correctly eighty-four percent of the time, against one hundred percent for the lab. Near a decision cut-off, confirm in the central lab.

scenes.title: Speed is not survival; verify before reporting
scenes.altText: Trial card (RATPAC, six UK EDs, 2243 patients with suspected MI): a point-of-care panel (CK-MB, myoglobin, troponin I at baseline and 90 minutes) raised successful discharge home from 13% to 32% and cut median initial stay from 14.2 to 8.8 h, but major adverse events did not differ (3% vs 2%), mean stay and inpatient days did not differ, and the panel cost more. A review notes little direct evidence that POCT improves ACS outcomes; another notes older POC troponin methods are less sensitive than central-lab high-sensitivity assays. Verification card (US CLIA 42 CFR 493.1253): before reporting patient results on an unmodified FDA-cleared non-waived test system, the lab must show it matches the manufacturer’s accuracy, precision and reportable range and check the reference intervals fit its patients; a modified or lab-developed method needs more, including analytical sensitivity and specificity. Waived tests: follow the manufacturer’s instructions (493.15(e)). A hospital POCT programme validated devices following CLSI guidance with comparison against central-lab analyzers. Hook-answer card.

cues.text: In a UK trial of over two thousand chest pain patients, a bedside cardiac marker panel more than doubled same-day discharge and cut the median stay. But major adverse events did not differ, and the panel cost more.
Reviews agree: little direct evidence of better outcomes in acute coronary syndrome, and older bedside troponin methods are less sensitive than central-lab high-sensitivity assays.

Before reporting, a new non-waived test system must be verified under US CLIA: accuracy, precision and reportable range comparable to the manufacturer’s, and reference intervals that fit the patients. Waived tests must follow the manufacturer’s instructions.
Back to the hook. The strip: dilute, repeat and confirm with quantitative hCG. The creatinine: confirm in the lab. The panel: faster, not proven to save lives. The analyzer: verify first.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “25 mIU/mL is the universal urine hCG cut-off” (✓ thresholds are device-specific; follow the named assay’s instructions; serum quantitative hCG has its own intervals); “POC cardiac markers improved ACS outcomes” (✓ they sped discharge and shortened median stay, but adverse events did not differ); “A borderline fingerstick creatinine is good enough” (✓ confirm near decision cut-offs in the central laboratory).

cues.text: Trap one: twenty-five units is the universal urine hCG cut-off. No: each device has its own threshold, so follow that assay’s instructions.
Trap two: bedside cardiac markers improved outcomes. No: they sped up discharge, but adverse events did not differ.
Trap three: a borderline fingerstick creatinine is good enough. No: near a decision cut-off, confirm it in the central lab.

scenes.title: The scout and the judge
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “A bedside result is a SCOUT, not a JUDGE: it reports fast, but near the border the central lab rules. Scouts bring speed, not survival — and every new scout is checked before it is trusted.” Tokens: scout = POCT · judge = central lab · check the scout = verify first. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: a bedside result is a scout, not a judge. It reports fast, but near the border the central lab rules. Scouts bring speed, not survival, and every new scout is checked before it is trusted.

Where it breaks: speed did change care, with more same-day discharges; confirmation rules come from the device instructions and local policy, not a slogan; and devices differ, so some bedside results agree well with the lab.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Urine hCG threshold = that device’s insert · doesn’t fit → dilute, repeat, confirm · borderline fingerstick creatinine → central lab”, “POC cardiac panel: faster discharge, no outcome difference · verify accuracy, precision, range before reporting”.

cues.text: Treat a bedside result as a fast scout: read a urine pregnancy strip by its own insert and confirm when it does not fit, send borderline fingerstick creatinine to the central lab, remember that bedside cardiac markers bought speed rather than better outcomes, and verify any new non-waived system before reporting.

props.label: hCG: that device’s insert · doesn’t fit → dilute, confirm · borderline creat → lab
POC cardiac panel: speed, not outcomes · verify before reporting

explanation.what: Plain language: bedside tests are fast, but each has limits. A pregnancy strip only says yes or no above its own threshold, and can be falsely negative; a fingerstick kidney test can be off by enough to put a patient on the wrong side of a cut-off; and getting cardiac results faster sent more people home sooner without changing how many had serious heart events. New tests must be checked before they report patient results. Scientific terms: qualitative lateral-flow immunoassay, analytical sensitivity (detection threshold), hook effect, hCG beta-core fragment, capillary versus plasma creatinine, eGFR misclassification, successful discharge, major adverse cardiac events, verification of performance specifications (accuracy, precision, reportable range, reference intervals).
explanation.why: Device thresholds and antibody designs differ, so no single number fits every strip. Very high or variant hCG can defeat the antibody sandwich. Small creatinine bias and imprecision matter most near a cut-off. Faster results change workflow, but outcomes depend on what is done with them. Verification shows the lab can reproduce the manufacturer’s performance in its own hands.
explanation.measure: Urine hCG kits: most ~25–50 mIU/mL, range 15–100 mIU/mL (one review); about half of German home tests missed their claim. CLIA: visual urine pregnancy tests are waived (493.15(c)(4)); waived labs follow manufacturer instructions (493.15(e)). Fingerstick creatinine: mean bias +12.7 µmol/L with misclassification at all CKD stages (Nataatmadja 2020); eGFR < 60 concordance 84% capillary vs 100% lab (Lemoine 2022). RATPAC: successful discharge 32% vs 13%; median stay 8.8 vs 14.2 h; adverse events 3% vs 2% (no significant difference). CLIA 493.1253: accuracy, precision, reportable range, reference intervals before reporting.
explanation.differs: Qualitative urine hCG (device threshold, line or no line) vs quantitative serum hCG (number, lab intervals); efficiency outcomes (discharge, median stay) vs clinical outcomes (adverse events); verification of an unmodified FDA-cleared test vs establishment of specifications for a modified or lab-developed test; waived (follow instructions) vs non-waived (verify).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: reject a “universal” urine hCG cut-off, pick dilution or quantitative testing for a suspected hook effect, choose central-lab confirmation for a borderline fingerstick creatinine, state that POC cardiac markers improved speed but not ACS outcomes, or list CLIA verification characteristics.

questions.stem: An ED patient with a uterus much larger than dates and suspected molar pregnancy has a negative qualitative urine hCG strip. What is the best next step?

options.text: Repeat on diluted urine and confirm with quantitative hCG, telling the lab a mole is suspected so the sample is diluted
options.rationale: Correct. Very high hCG can cause a hook-effect false negative; dilution often overcomes it, and the lab should be told so the quantitative assay is run on a diluted sample.
Incorrect. The clinical picture does not fit; a hook effect or hCG variant can give a false-negative strip.

options.text: Repeat the same undiluted strip until it turns positive
options.rationale: Incorrect. Repeating undiluted urine leaves the antigen excess in place.

options.text: Reinterpret the strip using a 25 mIU/mL universal cut-off
options.rationale: Incorrect. A strip gives no number, and thresholds are device-specific; there is no universal cut-off.

questions.stem: In the RATPAC randomised trial, what did a point-of-care cardiac marker panel in the emergency department change?

options.text: It increased successful discharge home and shortened median stay, without a difference in major adverse events
options.rationale: Correct. Successful discharge rose from 13% to 32% and median initial stay fell, but adverse events did not differ significantly.

options.text: It reduced deaths from acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: Incorrect. Major adverse events did not differ; reviews note little direct evidence of better ACS outcomes.
Incorrect. Mean cost was higher with the panel, and it was judged unlikely to be cost-effective.

options.text: It reduced mean inpatient days over follow-up
options.rationale: Incorrect. Mean inpatient days (1.8 vs 1.7) and mean initial stay did not differ.

questions.stem: A US laboratory introduces an unmodified, FDA-cleared, non-waived point-of-care analyzer. Under CLIA, what must it do before reporting patient results?

options.text: Show accuracy, precision and reportable range comparable to the manufacturer’s, and verify the reference intervals suit its patients
options.rationale: Correct. These are the verification requirements of 42 CFR 493.1253(b)(1).

options.text: Nothing, because FDA clearance replaces local verification
options.rationale: Incorrect. CLIA requires the laboratory to verify performance in its own hands before reporting.

options.text: Establish analytical sensitivity and specificity from scratch as for a lab-developed test
options.rationale: Incorrect. Full establishment is required for modified or lab-developed tests, not for an unmodified FDA-cleared system.

options.text: Only follow the manufacturer’s instructions, as for a waived test
options.rationale: Incorrect. Following instructions is the waived-test requirement; a non-waived system needs verification.

references.citation: Almoradie A. MEMORY LAB: The Memory-First Medical Laboratory Science Reviewer. 1st ed., v2.0. 2026. Chapter 7, Testing at the Bedside (EPUB; no fixed page numbers).
references.usedFor: Curriculum source: scope and exam framing. Not used as verification.

references.citation: Gnoth C, Johnson S. Strips of Hope: Accuracy of Home Pregnancy Tests and New Developments. Geburtshilfe Frauenheilkd. 2014;74(7):661-669. doi:10.1055/s-0034-1368589
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool (Europe PMC full text was empty). Laboratory performance of home urine hCG tests differs; about half of tests sold in Germany did not show their claimed sensitivity; testing too early is the most common cause of inaccurate (false-negative) results; hCG forms in urine including beta-core fragment.

references.citation: Priyadarshini S, Manas F, Prabhu S. False Negative Urine Pregnancy Test: Hook Effect Revealed. Cureus. 2022;14(3):e22779. doi:10.7759/cureus.22779
references.usedFor: Most kits detect hCG at 25–50 mIU/mL, others 15–100 mIU/mL; variants (free beta, beta-core) can prevent sandwich formation and give false negatives; hook effect; dilution before repeating often overcomes it; repeat with dilution and confirm when in doubt.

references.citation: Winder AD, Mora AS, Berry E, Lurain JR. The "hook effect" causing a negative pregnancy test in a patient with an advanced molar pregnancy. Gynecol Oncol Rep. 2017;21:34-36. doi:10.1016/j.gore.2017.06.008
references.usedFor: Very high hCG in molar pregnancy can cause a hook-effect false negative; suspicion should be communicated to the laboratory so a diluted sample is used.

references.citation: Nataatmadja M, Fung AWS, Jacobson B, et al. Performance of StatSensor Point-of-Care Device for Measuring Creatinine in Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease and Postkidney Transplantation. Can J Kidney Health Dis. 2020;7:2054358120970716. doi:10.1177/2054358120970716
references.usedFor: Fingerstick vs plasma creatinine: positive mean bias 12.7 µmol/L; eGFR misclassification across all KDIGO stages; bias correction did not fix it; imprecision as well as bias limits clinical use.

references.citation: Lemoine S, Rouveure AC, Dubourg L, et al. Point of care creatinine derived eGFR measurement in capillary blood for identifying patients at risk. Pract Lab Med. 2022;31:e00296. doi:10.1016/j.plabm.2022.e00296
references.usedFor: For measured GFR < 60, concordance 84% (capillary), 88% (venous) vs 100% (laboratory creatinine); falsely flagged patients clarified with follow-up laboratory testing. Device supplied by the manufacturer.

references.citation: Goodacre SW, Bradburn M, Cross E, Collinson P, Gray A, Hall AS; RATPAC Research Team. The Randomised Assessment of Treatment using Panel Assay of Cardiac Markers (RATPAC) trial: a randomised controlled trial of point-of-care cardiac markers in the emergency department. Heart. 2011;97(3):190-196. doi:10.1136/hrt.2010.203166
references.usedFor: Abstract only (via Europe PMC), together with the abstract of the HTA report (Goodacre S, et al. Health Technol Assess. 2011;15(23):iii-xi, 1-102. doi:10.3310/hta15230; NIHR full text returned HTTP 403). Six UK EDs, 2243 patients; panel of CK-MB, myoglobin and troponin I at 0 and 90 min; successful discharge 32% vs 13%; median stay 8.8 vs 14.2 h; no difference in mean stay, inpatient days or major adverse events (3% vs 2%); higher mean cost, unlikely to be cost-effective.

references.citation: Rooney KD, Schilling UM. Point-of-care testing in the overcrowded emergency department--can it make a difference? Crit Care. 2014;18(6):692. doi:10.1186/s13054-014-0692-9
references.usedFor: Cardiac biomarker POCT shortens TAT and length of stay; little direct evidence that POCT in ACS results in superior outcomes. Industry-funded review.

references.citation: Shaw JLV. Practical challenges related to point of care testing. Pract Lab Med. 2016;4:22-29. doi:10.1016/j.plabm.2015.12.002
references.usedFor: POC troponin methods lack analytical sensitivity compared with central-lab high-sensitivity troponin assays.

references.citation: Khan AH, Shakeel S, Hooda K, Siddiqui K, Jafri L. Best Practices in the Implementation of a Point of Care Testing Program: Experience From a Tertiary Care Hospital in a Developing Country. EJIFCC. 2019;30(3):288-302.
references.usedFor: POCT method validation per CLSI guidelines at the central laboratory: accuracy, precision, reportable range, inter-instrument comparison and comparison with central-lab benchtop analyzers.

references.citation: 42 CFR § 493.15 — Laboratories performing waived tests (eCFR, version current to 2026-10-01).
references.usedFor: Waived list includes non-automated dipstick urinalysis and visual colour-comparison urine pregnancy tests; waived laboratories must follow manufacturers’ instructions.

references.citation: 42 CFR § 493.1253 — Standard: Establishment and verification of performance specifications (eCFR, version current to 2026-10-01).
references.usedFor: Before reporting, unmodified FDA-cleared systems: verify accuracy, precision, reportable range, reference intervals; modified or lab-developed: establish specifications including analytical sensitivity and specificity; document all. Subpart K applies to non-waived testing (493.1200(a)).

claims.text: Urine hCG thresholds are device-specific (most 25–50, range 15–100 mIU/mL); many home tests miss claimed sensitivity; waived labs follow manufacturer instructions.
False-negative causes: testing too early; hook effect at very high hCG; hCG variants; dilute, repeat and confirm; tell the lab when a mole is suspected.
Fingerstick creatinine bias, imprecision and eGFR misclassification; confirm near decision cut-offs in the central laboratory.

POC cardiac panel: more successful discharge, shorter median stay, no difference in adverse events, higher cost; little direct evidence of better ACS outcomes; POC troponin less sensitive than high-sensitivity central-lab assays.
CLIA verification before reporting (accuracy, precision, reportable range, reference intervals); establishment for modified tests; POCT validation with central-lab comparison following CLSI.
QuickVue 25 mIU/mL specification; 10–20 specimens for simple manual POCT validation; “not ideal” fingerstick quote; Number Vault figures.
claims.note: Not taught as facts; the QuidelOrtho product page could not be retrieved and no source read states the specimen number.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 7 Hit 10 states that simple manual POCT such as urine dipsticks is validated on 10–20 specimens. No source read in this session gives that number, and US CLIA lists non-automated dipstick urinalysis as a waived test whose only analytic requirement is following the manufacturer’s instructions (42 CFR 493.15); formal verification under 493.1253 applies to non-waived systems. The number is likely a local or accreditation practice (register flag rv-ch7-dipstick-validation-size).

Ch. 7 Hit 9 says POCT cardiac markers improved ED efficiency without evidence of outcome effect. The RATPAC trial supports the outcome point but qualifies efficiency: successful discharge and median stay improved, while mean stay and inpatient days did not change and cost was higher (register flag rv-ch7-poc-cardiac-efficiency).
The waived-test and verification rules taught here are US federal (CLIA) requirements. Philippine laboratory licensing and POCT rules are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local requirements.
